proposed.headline: Z.AI's $5 billion, inspected.
proposed.your_call_question: Z.AI just raised $5 billion, $3 billion of it as a bond due next year. Is this money still here in eighteen months?
proposed.check_note: Checked on all three lenses: the evidence exists and is attributed, the format boundary holds, and the voice is not preaching.
proposed.check_detail: Route: Reuters returned 401 to curl and a Cloudflare challenge via r.jina.ai; Bamboo Works returned 403 on both routes; archive.ph reset the connection. Only Caixin was directly readable (curl with a browser UA, HTTP 200), plus a WebSearch pass that surfaced the Reuters wire in syndication (The Standard, Business Standard, Express Tribune, MarketScreener, Qz). Figure by figure: the $5bn TOTAL is CONFIRMED by a named producer, Caixin, byline Yang Zirui, 14 Sep 2026, human-written lede: 'raised about HK$39.3 billion ($5 billion) through a share placement and a concurrent convertible bond sale', and corroborated by the Reuters headline itself ('raises $5 billion... filing shows'), which sources to an HKEX filing, so lens item 1 passes on a filing plus two bylined outlets, not an aggregator stub. The ~$2bn PLACEMENT at 22 million H shares and HK$714 is CONFIRMED but with a sourcing caveat and one numeric correction: the figures ('offered 21.97 million shares at HK$714 each') sit in Caixin's Digest Hub / Who's Who panels, which the page explicitly labels 'AI generated, for reference only', not in its human-written free text; HK$714 is independently corroborated by the syndicated Reuters copy ('a 25 percent premium to the HK$714 share placement price'), and the arithmetic reconciles (21.97m x HK$714 = HK$15.69bn = ~$2.0bn). The ~$3bn CONVERTIBLE is CONFIRMED by two independent routes that agree on the same yuan figure: Caixin's panel ('issued 20.14 billion yuan in bonds') and the syndicated Reuters copy ('20.14 billion yuan (HK$23.55 billion) of zero-coupon bonds due in September 2027'); HK$39.3bn total minus HK$15.69bn placement = HK$23.6bn, which closes the loop. ZERO-COUPON, DUE 2027 and CONVERSION PRICE HK$892.50 are corroborated only through the search engine's rendering of syndicated Reuters text, not from any page I could open and archive, and I am flagging that plainly rather than calling them read. HK$892.50 is exactly HK$714 x 1.25, matching the reported 25% premium, so it is arithmetically self-consistent, and Caixin's free text independently proves I am not pattern-matching a different deal: 'zero-coupon convertible bond' appears attributed to MiniMax for the July raise, NOT to Z.AI, so treat zero-coupon-for-Z.AI as corroborated but unread. No figure here needs evidence that must be CREATED: this is a filing-reading piece, so lens item 3 passes cleanly. Corrections the record needs before drafting: (1) '22 million H shares' is 21.97 million, so write 'about 22 million' or use the precise number; (2) the bond is yuan-denominated (20.14bn yuan / HK$23.55bn) and settled in US dollars, so '$3 billion' is an FX translation, not a fixed dollar liability, which is material for a split.the.bill piece whose whole hinge is the size of a debt; (3) the machine's reason says 'a fixed maturity decides the verdict', which is incomplete: the syndicated copy reports an issuer call from 18 February 2027 if shares trade at or above 130% of the conversion price for 20 of 30 trading days, so maturity is not the only date that settles it; (4) the bonds were issued at 100.5% of face, a zero-coupon priced above par, a negative yield to maturity for holders and worth one line; (5) the your.call's eighteen-month horizon (to about March 2028) sits past the September 2027 maturity, which is coherent, so keep it; (6) before print, pull the HKEX filing itself or a readable syndication (The Standard or Business Standard both resolved in search) so the three bond terms have a directly read, archived source rather than a search summary.

proposed.headline: The frontier premium, inspected.
proposed.your_call_question: Mozilla says paying for a frontier model buys a four-month head start at five times the cost per task. What does that head start really cost, and who ends up holding the bill?
proposed.check_note: Checked on all three lenses: the evidence exists and is attributed, the format boundary holds, and the voice is not preaching.
proposed.check_detail: The claim and both numbers exist today and are attributed to named producers, and the piece needs no bench, survey or experiment to be built. Verified chain: (1) The candidate URL, Ars Technica, byline Jeremy Hsu, published 2026-09-15, headline "Exclusive: Paying for frontier AI models buys 4-month head start at 5x the cost". It states the gap "has closed to just 4.4 months, according to a Mozilla report", quotes Raffi Krikorian, Mozilla CTO, by email, and attributes the per-task cost to Vals AI's Terminal-Bench 2.1 run: GLM 5.2 "costing about five times less per completed task" than Claude Opus 4.7 and 4.8. Hsu's own summary sentence, "about a four-month head start at about five times the per-task cost, but only when currently looking at tasks taking between eight and 12 hours", is the candidate claim almost word for word. WebFetch was blocked on arstechnica.com, so I fetched it with curl through the proxy and read the full article text. (2) Independent corroboration: Tom's Hardware, byline Shane Downing, 2026-09-16, reports the same 4.4 months (Mozilla fit on METR data, in line with Epoch AI's four months) and "less than one-fifth the cost per test". (3) Primary source: stateofopensource.ai, "The State of Open Source AI, v1.1, September 2026", with Raffi Krikorian's letter and an 8-page PDF at stateofopensource.ai/state-of-open-source-ai-v1-1.pdf (downloaded, 8.3 MB, valid PDF). The report's own text reads "≈4.4 mo measured open–closed lag (Mozilla fit on METR data); Epoch: 4 months" and "On a neutral harness, the price gap is 5×, Terminal-Bench 2.1 on vals.ai". The 30% token-price figure cites "Artificial Analysis; vendor pricing pages, Aug 2026". The "who holds the bill" half of the question also has existing evidence: Krikorian on why organisations still pay closed (compliance packaging, support, accountability), the DoorDash split, the Linux Foundation revenue split (Frank Nagle and Daniel Yue: open 4%, closed 96%, May to Sept 2025), and Tom's Hardware's hardware caveat (the price comparison is API to API at list price; Kimi K3 needs about 1.5 TB and 64 or more accelerators to self-host, so "open but not runnable by most who hold it"). Archive note, which is the candidate's existing source_archive_needed gate and not a fail: the candidate URL is a dated news article, not a pricing page, but the 5x figure sits on live boards that have already moved since the report's 1 September data cut (the Artificial Analysis Terminal-Bench 2.1 page now lists Fable 5.1 at 91.4%, and Tom's says the vals.ai board updated 11 September now leads with GPT-6 Astra), and the Mozilla blog URL both outlets link still serves the July 14 v1.0 post. Before recording, archive the v1.1 PDF, the stateofopensource.ai page, the Ars and Tom's articles, and dated snapshots of the vals.ai and Artificial Analysis Terminal-Bench 2.1 boards. Two caveats the writer should carry rather than hide: the 5x per-task comparison is GLM 5.2 against Opus 4.7 and 4.8, not against Fable 5, and Ars and Tom's disagree slightly on the Opus 4.8 gap (within a point versus about four points), so quote the report's chart, not either paraphrase; and Mozilla is an open-model advocate whose CTO called the report partly advocacy (TIME, July 14), which the piece should say. Source refs used: the two candidate URLs plus f2fbe93a-0173-4901-85aa-0b9b120549cb, which is the idea row id, not a URL, so nothing to fetch there.

proposed.headline: The 72-hour breach, inspected.
proposed.your_call_question: Three researchers, a rival's model, under 3,000 dollars in tokens and OpenAI's internal GitHub in 72 hours: what is actually happening to lab security, against what everyone says is happening?
proposed.check_note: Checked on all three lenses: the evidence exists and is attributed, the format boundary holds, and the voice is not preaching.
proposed.check_detail:
Both load bearing numbers are on the page and attributed to a named producer. Hacktron AI published the post on 13 September 2026 under three named researchers: Harsh Jaiswal, Mohan Pedhapati and Rahul Maini. The page says "OpenAI also paid us a $6,500 bounty" and "The whole HEIF Heist research project going after Slack, Meta, adn more took two-months, cost less than $3,000 in tokens in total, and was conducted by three researchers" (the typo is in the original). The under 72 hours route into OpenAI's internal monorepo is there too, as a PR opened in openai/openai via an employee's Codex. So the piece can be written from evidence that exists today, and the money side holds.

Two fixes the writer has to make, neither of them a missing evidence problem. First, the 3,000 dollars covers the whole two month campaign across several targets, not the OpenAI break in on its own, so the headline "A 3,000 dollar break in, priced" claims more than the source supports. Say what the number actually covers. Second, the candidate snippet says Opus 5 produced the exploit "in about three hours". That figure is not on the page. The page says Opus 4.8 struggled across several sessions to get a working exploit with ASLR enabled, and that Opus 5 succeeded within hours of its release. Drop the three hours or reword it to match.

Two caveats to carry into the draft. The token cost and the bounty are both self reported by the team that did the work, so attribute them to Hacktron rather than stating them flat. And the other half of the bill, what OpenAI, Slack or Meta spent on remediation, is not on the page and I found no public figure for it. The piece has to leave that as the open question, which is what the your call question already does, and must not put a number on it.

On archiving: the url is a research blog post, not a pricing page, a changelog or a docs page, so the source_not_archived handoff does not apply. It is still a vendor page that can be edited or pulled, and the two figures are the whole argument, so archiving it the way c0037 and c0038 were archived is worth doing before recording.

proposed.headline: The last AI built by humans, inspected: 491 papers on a five-rung ladder.
proposed.your_call_question: Everyone says AI is about to build its own successors. Of 491 papers on the subject, where does the work actually sit?
proposed.check_note: Checked on all three lenses: the evidence exists and is attributed, the format boundary holds, and the voice is not preaching.
proposed.check_detail: Could not refute. The evidence exists today in one primary source and I checked it directly. WebFetch returned only the PDF's compressed streams, so I downloaded the PDF (7.8 MB, HTTP 200) and the abstract page with curl and extracted the text locally with pypdf (79 pages). Verified: arXiv 2609.11873, title "The Last AI Built by Humans: Toward Genuine Recursive Self-Improvement", submitted 10 Sep 2026, revised 15 Sep 2026 (v2), 36 named authors. Figure 18 in Appendix A gives "Distribution of 491 surveyed papers" by autonomy level: L1 215 (43.8%), L2 155 (31.6%), L3 64 (13.0%), L4 28 (5.7%), L5 29 (5.9%); the counts sum to 491. L1 plus L2 is 370 of 491, which is 75.4 percent, so "75 percent on the bottom two rungs" holds. L5 is 29 of 491, which is 5.9 percent, so "under 6 percent at the top" holds. The five-level ladder is the paper's own framework (section 3, "we review RSI techniques across five levels"). The "everyone says" side is also sourced inside the paper: it cites Anthropic Institute, "When AI builds itself" (June 2026, accessed 2026-09-08), describing the strongest form as "an AI system autonomously designing and developing its own successor", plus OpenAI [68], Tencent [69] and Alibaba [30]. The authors' own words support the gap: "end-to-end L5 evidence is concentrated in bounded prototypes" and "L5 evolution of the improver itself remain[s] largely unexplored". arXiv is a permanent versioned archive, so no source_not_archived handoff; record the version as v2 and the figure as Figure 18, since v2 already replaced v1 and a v3 could renumber. Three corrections the writer must carry. First, attribution: the newsletter's "ByteDance, Tsinghua and Shanghai AI Lab" is partial. The lead affiliations are Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Theseus Labs (the corresponding author Xuanhe Zhou sits there); ByteDance, Tsinghua and Shanghai AI Lab are secondary among ten institutions. Second, the paper does not cite I. J. Good or the 1965 intelligence explosion anywhere; its own lineage runs through Schmidhuber's Gödel machine [14] and the Darwin Gödel Machine [16]. Good 1965 is a real published paper (Advances in Computers, vol. 6) so the trace can be written from existing evidence, but it must be sourced separately and the piece must not say the paper traces to Good. Third, the level percentages are by paper count and the paper's B0 baseline is not one of the 491, so "five rungs" is exact and "six" would be wrong. The producer is named (OpenAI), and the day one gap the piece wants to inspect is stated by OpenAI itself, so nothing has to be created and no bench, survey or experiment is needed. Every number now traces to the producer's page rather than to a second hand retelling. Archiving is done, so there is no source handoff: the live url returns HTTP 403 to WebFetch and to curl from this session, but that is a bot block and not a missing page, since openai.com/index/ answers the same way, and ten Wayback snapshots exist between 17 and 19 September. Second, Harvey and Legora are named as API customers who will build on Astra for Law, not as plugin partners; the named plugin partners are iManage, Intapp, DeepJudge and Thomson Reuters. suggestions.title: The UN's 21 percent, inspected.
suggestions.reason:
The cited url does not carry the spine. I fetched the Google blog post (Prem Ramaswami, Head of Data Commons, 17 Sep 2026) and read it in full. It confirms the first half of the claim: the UN System Data Commons is built on Google's open source Data Commons, it supports MCP, AI agents can fetch figures from it directly, and the UN targets 80 percent of its statistical datasets by 2027. It contains no accuracy figure, no 21 percent, and no UNICEF measurement of any kind. UNICEF appears once, in passing, in a line about a child poverty report. A writer following the recorded evidence_refs would print a number their source does not contain.

The number does exist today, but at a different source and in a weaker form than the claim states. TechCrunch (Jagmeet Singh, 17 Sep 2026) reports a UNICEF benchmark of six models across more than 133,000 responses with an average accuracy score of 21.2 percent, given by João Pedro Azevedo, UNICEF's chief statistician, in a virtual press briefing. The models named are GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash and Gemini 2.0 Flash. The same report states the study is a UNICEF working paper being prepared for journal submission, not yet peer reviewed, with methodology, code and data promised but not released. I searched for a primary UNICEF document and found none. Every public trace of the figure leads back to that one briefing.

Two further problems. The claim restates the finding as models answering correctly only 21 percent of the time, which is not what was measured: it was an average accuracy score, and about three in five responses gave no usable number at all. And the piece promises to inspect the world's numbers while its own central number cannot be inspected by anyone outside UNICEF.

This is not a kill, and the evidence does not have to be created: UNICEF ran the bench, it is simply unreleased. The path to a pass is to add the briefing report as the ref for the number, attribute it to Azevedo by name with the date, say plainly that the paper is not out and not peer reviewed, and lean on the two figures that are easier to stand behind, three in five answers with no usable number, and repeat runs two days later agreeing only about half the time. I default to false here because the recorded evidence does not support the spine as written.

suggestions.title: 25,000 robotaxis, inspected.
suggestions.reason:
The event is real and well sourced, but the question the piece asks is not answerable from anything published today.

What I checked. The FT link in the candidate could not be fetched (FT is hard paywalled and the fetch was refused), so I confirmed the claim against other named producers instead. TechCrunch, Electrek and InsideEVs all carry the Lucid and Bolt announcement of 17 September 2026 for at least 25,000 autonomous vehicles on Lucid's midsize platform, running Nvidia Hyperion and aimed at SAE Level 4. TechCrunch quotes the press release that Bolt intends to own and operate the fleet. So the claim and the 25,000 number are confirmed and attributed.

Why it still fails. The your-call question has two halves. The second half, who holds the bill, has a published answer: Bolt's autonomous driving unit owns and operates. The first half, what one robotaxi costs to put on the road, has no source at all. TechCrunch states plainly that no money has changed hands and Bolt has not placed an order, and every report says no deal value was disclosed. There is no per-vehicle price, no capital commitment and no cost breakdown anywhere in the record. Lucid's roughly $50,000 midsize target is for the consumer car, not the Midsize Plus robotaxi build with the AV hardware bolted on, and that car does not start production until late 2028. Nvidia does not publish a Hyperion sensor and compute price. To cost one robotaxi the writer would have to build the figure from parts that are either unannounced or unpriced, then run the piece on a spreadsheet estimate presented as the headline number. That is a number created for the piece, not evidence that exists today, which is why the gate material_exists should read false for the cost side even though it is true for the event.

Two further traps for whoever picks this up. The FT url should not be the citation because neither the writer nor a reader can open it; the Lucid investor relations release and TechCrunch cover the same facts and are open. And Lucid already has a separate 25,000 unit minimum quantity guarantee with Uber from April 2026, so a piece headlined "twenty five thousand robotaxis" can easily merge two different commitments from the same carmaker.

Suggested corrected format. A version that does work on today's record is the gap between what Lucid has promised (two separate lots of 25,000) and what it actually built last year, reported as 18,378 cars. Treat that last figure as a lead, not verified: I saw it only in a search headline and it needs checking at Lucid's own filings before use.

On the standing instruction about fable: nothing uses it. Across the repo the string appears only inside defensive regexes, at /home/user/control-center/api/_models.ts (THINKS_BY_DEFAULT), /home/user/control-center/api/_content.ts (NO_SAMPLING_MODELS) and /home/user/control-center/scripts/check-model-routing.mts (the MODEL pattern). No call site selects claude-fable-5, and PROXY_ALLOWED_MODELS does not list it. No Fable model was used in this run.

The same page gives "over 23 million exchanges observed" as the total distillation activity attributable to Moonshot between May and July 2026. The revenue side is Bloomberg reporting (11 September), carried by TechCrunch (Russell Brandom) and Channel Insider: a $2 billion annualised target by year end, run rate over $1 billion in August, up from $300 million in June. Moonshot has not responded (Bloomberg: did not respond; Dealroom: has not addressed it). Two problems. First, the candidate's question says "23 million of Kimi's exchanges ran through Claude", which misreads the source: the 23 million is Moonshot's total distillation exchanges with Claude, and the figure for Kimi users actually served Claude is the 300,000 in one ten day window. The 66-page complaint, Alvarez v. Meta Platforms, 1:26-cv-10773 (N.D. Ill., filed 4 Sep 2026), is public on CourtListener; I downloaded it and searched the full text. Meta's 2 Nov 2021 post (Jerome Pesenti) is live. None of these is a pricing, changelog or docs page, so no archive is needed. Refuted: the piece's premise. The candidate says the complaint alleges the 2021 faceprints were "kept and reused". It does not. The complaint never mentions the November 2021 shutdown, the billion-template deletion, DeepFace or Pesenti (zero hits for each). Its theory is fresh extraction from photos uploaded since 4 Sep 2021, pleaded "upon information and belief". Wired itself writes that it "could not determine where the underlying faceprint data came from", and the complaint only says the NameTag faceprints are "possibly derived" from Facebook and Instagram images. Meta's reply is "we are not building a universal face database". So the headline "Meta's deleted faceprints, inspected" and the your_call question "what is actually happening to the faceprints Meta said it deleted" have no evidence on the "actually happening" side: nobody outside Meta has inspected those templates, no filing alleges they survived, and the answer sits inside Meta or in discovery that has not happened. A mind_the_gap piece needs the real state to be documentable; here only the 2021 promise is. Inferred, not verified: the class period starting 4 Sep 2021 looks like the five-year BIPA lookback from the filing date rather than anything to do with the deletion (the complaint gives no reason). A different gap could be written today from documents that exist (the 2021 promise, Facebook Verified launching on facial embeddings in July 2026 with unstated retention, and a complaint alleging new faceprints built since), but that is a different question and headline, so this candidate fails as written.

suggestions.reason: The source is real and has a named producer, but the claim as written is not in it and neither is a number. The url resolves to Liquid AI's engineering blog post "Setting the Frontier of Aging Biology with Liquid Foundation Models", dated 17 September 2026, which credits Insilico Medicine for the collaboration and cites a Cell Press manuscript by Zhavoronkov, Alex, et al. It is a blog post, not a pricing page, changelog or docs page, so no archive gate applies, and a local copy was saved anyway at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-control-center/6c3d966a-1816-585c-8f36-8d23bd6fee46/scratchpad/slate/c0042_liquid_longevitybench.html and .txt. Three problems. First, attribution: the page never names GPT-5, Gemini or Claude. A search of the full 15,376 character page text returns zero hits for "Gemini" and zero for "Claude", and the only two "GPT" hits are bibliography citations to scGPT and CpGPT, which are unrelated papers. What the page actually says is "We compared our Longevity-LLMs with 18 frontier LLMs" and that on three named tasks the LFM2 models "outperformed every frontier model evaluated". Those 18 models are not listed here, so "topped GPT-5, Gemini and Claude" cannot be sourced from this url. Second, there is no number. The page gives ordinal ranks only, second and fourth, with zero hits for "accuracy" and zero for "score", and it states that the complete benchmark results sit in the Cell Press paper, which this check did not open. Third, the angle itself is weakened by the page: the best overall rank in the family went to L-Qwen3.5-9B, a domain-adapted 9B Qwen, not to either of the two small LFM2 models. So the real finding is that domain fine-tuning beats scale, not that two small models beat the frontier labs on their own ground, which is the spine of the proposed piece. A piece on this topic can be written from evidence that exists today, so this is not a case of evidence having to be created, but this claim and this number cannot be written from the cited url. To proceed, open the Cell Press paper, name the frontier models it actually tested, and carry a real score rather than a rank.
